title: Autoscaling a custom resource which does not create pods
body:
If someone has a custom resource which does not create pods but does have a scale subresource, it would be nice to be able to scale it based only on a custom metric. Currently this is not possible with HorizontalPodAutoscaler since it needs to list pods and does not just trust what the scale subresource tells it.

This would mean ignoring the implementation details of whatever the custom resource controller creates under the hood and just use the status of the scale subresource.

(obviously this means the "pod" in the hpa name wouldn't make much sense, but raising this so it could be considered if other changes happen around the area of counting pods)

title: Proposing unification and alignment of apiserver storage metrics (etcd3 and watch cache)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, Kubernetes exposes separate sets of metrics for etcd3 or from the watch cache. Both implement exactly the same interface and methods, but they have totally different metrics. For example, etcd3 exports metric with `apiserver_storage_list_total`,  while the cacher exposes `apiserver_cache_list_total`.

We propose to unify these aligned metrics by introducing a storage label. This would allow users to aggregate metrics across the entire storage layer or filter by specific backend (etcd or watchcache).

**Proposed label**: `storage="etcd|watchcache"`


For example, apiserver_storage_list_total could be unified with a label:

* apiserver_storage_list_total{storage="etcd"}
* apiserver_storage_list_total{storage="watchcache"}

Caveats and Recommendations
* gRPC Metrics vs. Storage Metrics: While etcd client calls are covered by gRPC-level metrics, these are often "unmergable" with application-level concepts like the watch cache. We recommend maintaining aligned metrics at the k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage layer to allow direct comparison of the same logical operations regardless of the serving layer.

## Next Steps

1. Complete the audit of all metrics in [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go) and [staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/metrics/metrics.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/metrics/metrics.go).
2. Agree on a final set of unified metric names and labels.
3. Define a deprecation path for the existing fragmented metrics.

### Why is this needed?

This fragmentation hinders observability by:
* Preventing a unified view of storage operations (e.g. type and percentage of request served from etcd).
* Violating [Prometheus best practices](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/#labels), which recommend using labels to differentiate characteristics of the thing being measured rather than embedding them in the metric name.

title: No clean way to apply feature-gate-gated metric options
body:
**Problem**

Some metric options (like [native histogram options](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0275382260bc0d5279b703d21ec7ad4db35b8d78/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/internal/nativehistograms.go#L33-L40) supported via `NativeHistograms` feature gate, potentially more in future) need to be applied at metric registration time. Specifically, `initializeMetric()` ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/histogram.go#L96)) reads `NativeHistogramsEnabled()` ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/opts.go#L210-L214)) when creating the underlying prometheus object, so feature gate state must be known before any metric is registered.
The problem here is that the current registration setup provides no clean way to guarantee this ordering. Metrics packages (workqueue, restclient, leaderelection, fifo) have historically registered themselves via `init()` which fires at import time, well before flags are parsed and feature gates are finalized.
______________________________

**What was tried**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137061 attempted to fix this by removing `init()` from those packages and requiring explicit `Register()` calls from each component's `Run()` function, after the feature gates are parsed. This works for in-tree components in `k/k` but introduces 2 problems:

1. Silent breakages for out-of-tree consumers
Projects outside `k/k` (operators, cloud provider controllers, anything using `client-go` or `controller-runtime`) relied on `init()` auto-registration. With it removed, their `workqueue_*`, `rest_client_*` etc. metrics silently disappear with no error or warning

2. `sync.Once` makes correct ordering impossible in practice
The new `Register()` functions use `sync.Once` to prevent double-registration panics, which creates a "first caller wins" problem. Consider an operator built on `controller-runtime`, to avoid breaking its own users, `controller-runtime` must call `Register()` early. That fires the `sync.Once` before feature gates are parsed. Later when the operator calls `Register()` after parsing the feature gates, the call is a silent no-op, consequently native-histograms never get enabled. There is no way for framework authors to avoid this. If they call `Register()` early they block the feature gate from taking effect, if they dont, some other `init()` in the dependency graph may do it instead.
This means the correctness of metric configuration now depends on non-deterministic `init()` ordering across the full transitive dependency graph.
______________________________

**Potential fixes**

1. defer prom metric object creations till after the feature-gates are parsed by making [`legacyregistry`
`legacyregistry.MustRegister`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/legacyregistry/registry.go#L37) enqueue metrics into a pending set rather than immediately calling `initializeMetric()`. When `ApplyFeatureGates()` is called, the registry flushes the pending set, firing `initializeMetric()` for every queued metric, now with the correct feature gate state set. POC: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138453
2. Move creation of metrics from init() funcs to constructors of the objects that use the metrics. This came up after discussion with @liggitt, who suggested a more principled alternative to the above solution -"if we really need to defer constructing metrics to be feature-gate informed, I'd rather just delay that directly instead of trying to allow them to still be constructed early, but held, and then really for real constructed later". POC: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138914


Would like to hear any other ideas to fix this issue, since addressing this will establish a clean way to use future feature-gated metric options reliably as well.

title: HPA tolerance check causes unexpected scale-up during rolling updates
body:
### What happened?


When using an External metric with `AverageValue` target, the HPA unintentionally scales up `spec.replicas` during rolling updates, even when the metric value indicates no scaling is needed.

During a rolling update, `status.replicas` temporarily exceeds `spec.replicas` due to surge pods. The HPA's tolerance check uses `statusReplicas` as both the divisor for ratio calculation and the return value when within tolerance. This causes `spec.replicas` to drift upward to match `status.replicas` without any actual load increase.

### Additional context

- The issue is most visible with tight `minReplicas`/`maxReplicas` ranges where even a +1 drift is significant
- Metric types using `Value` (not `AverageValue`) go through `GetExternalMetricReplicas` which has the same pattern and is likely affected as well
- The drift is bounded by `maxReplicas`, but causes unnecessary resource consumption and can interact poorly with custom controllers that set metric values based on `spec.replicas`

### Cascading impact: Cluster Autoscaler node thrashing

This bug can escalate from a pod-level issue to an infrastructure-level issue when combined with the Cluster Autoscaler (CA).

Consider the following scenario:

1. The Cluster Autoscaler decides to scale down a node (the node is underutilized)
2. Pods on the draining node enter `Terminating` state; replacement pods are scheduled to other nodes
3. During this transition, `status.replicas` temporarily exceeds `spec.replicas` (terminating pods + replacement pods both count toward status)
4. The HPA tolerance bug triggers: `spec.replicas` is bumped upward (e.g., 22 → 23)
5. This creates an **unexpected extra pod** that was not part of the original capacity plan
6. If the remaining nodes don't have enough capacity for this extra pod (since CA was in the process of *removing* a node, not adding one), the pod goes `Pending`
7. The `Pending` pod triggers the Cluster Autoscaler to scale **up** a new node

**Net result: A node scale-down operation triggers an unintended node scale-up.** The cluster oscillates — CA removes a node, HPA creates an extra pod, CA adds a node back — wasting infrastructure resources and causing unnecessary scheduling churn.

This is particularly impactful in environments with:
- Large pod resource requests (where a single extra pod can exceed remaining node capacity)
- Tight node capacity planning (nodes are close to full)
- Slow node provisioning (minutes of `Pending` state before the new node is ready)

### What did you expect to happen?

When the metric-derived ratio falls within the tolerance zone, the HPA should preserve the current `spec.replicas` (no scaling action), regardless of the transient `status.replicas` value.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**Setup:**

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  minReplicas: 22
  maxReplicas: 24
  metrics:
  - external:
      metric:
        name: my_custom_metric
      target:
        averageValue: "1"
        type: AverageValue
    type: External
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-deployment
```

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Deployment is stable: `spec.replicas = 22`, `status.replicas = 22`
2. External metric controller exposes metric value = 22 (meaning: 22 replicas desired, 1 per pod matches target)
3. Trigger a rolling update (e.g., change container image)
4. During rollout, `status.replicas = 23` due to maxSurge (surge pod created before old pod terminates)
5. HPA evaluates: `usageRatio = 22 / (1 × 23) = 0.957` → within 10% tolerance
6. HPA returns `statusReplicas = 23` as desired count
7. `23 > spec.replicas(22)` → **HPA patches spec.replicas to 23** (unintended scale-up)
8. Next cycle: `spec = 23`, `status = 24` (new surge) → same pattern → **spec drifts to 24**
9. Stops at `maxReplicas = 24`

**Observed: `spec.replicas` escalated 22 → 23 → 24 with zero load increase.**

title: client-go: rest_client metrics lack resource dimensions, making client-side observability difficult
body:
### What happened?

Server-side metrics (e.g. `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`) let you measure latency per verb, resource, group, version, and scope.

However, the client-side metrics exposed by client-go's REST layer use only verb (raw HTTP method) and host as labels. This means:

  - You cannot measure client-side latency per resource. "How long do Pod LIST calls take from the controller's perspective?" is unanswerable.
  - LIST and GET are indistinguishable. The client records the raw HTTP method GET for both. The server distinguishes these as separate verbs.
  - No scope information. You cannot distinguish cluster-scoped from namespace-scoped requests.

Debugging client-side latency is difficult because the metrics lack this information.

We could add resource-aware labels to `rest_client` metrics, similar to what server-side metrics already provide:

1. We could add resource , group, version, and scope labels.
2. We could map HTTP methods to API verbs (GET vs LIST) so verb carries semantic meaning.


Additionally, the recently introduced `A Unified Identity for client-go Components for Enhanced Telemetry` ([xref](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HUNewBqN3lk2DSHJaxKZmmhYgt0SNgp9AqpJTY6cfRM/edit?resourcekey=0-uIvQ3ezUROHa6OKjWZUzcw&tab=t.0#heading=h.qtaj715knfkg))  for client-go components provides a name label that Informers and Reflectors propagate to identify which component initiated a request. This identity could also be passed into rest_client metrics, allowing to correlate API requests back to the specific component that made them.

title: HPA controller - hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector func serializes all workers behind global exclusive mutex, causing ~ O(#Hpa*#Hpa) degradation at scale
body: ### What happened? ### TL;DR on the Issue The HPA controller's selector overlap check ([`hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L396-L422)) runs every reconciliation for every HPA and holds a [global exclusive mutex](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) while performing O(H) work. Despite starting [multiple worker goroutines](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L217), only one can execute the overlap check at a time. At scale, **_mutex contention_** dominates wall-clock time and reconciliation cannot keep up with the resync period. ### Mutex profile **60-second sample:** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Duration: 60.02s, Total samples = 1.35hrs (8111.81%) 1.35hrs 100% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).computeReplicasForMetrics 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.41%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.92%) ``` 1.35 hours of goroutine-blocked time accumulated in 60 seconds of wall clock (8111% of wall clock duration). **Cumulative snapshot (since process start):** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Total samples = 4.18hrs 4.18hrs 99.90% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.25%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.80%) ``` 99.25% of all mutex contention in the HPA controller is in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. ### Root cause Three problems compound: #### 1. Global exclusive lock on a per-HPA operation The [`hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L125) is held for the [entire body](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) of `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. This includes iterating all pods, inserting each into the BiMultimap, querying associations, and cleaning up. All worker goroutines contend on this single lock regardless of namespace. #### 2. BiMultimap cache is always cold [`KeepOnly([]Key{})`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415) destroys all temporary pod entries at the end of every call. This triggers [refCount decrement to zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L188-L191), which deletes the `selectingByLabeled` cache entry. Every subsequent call hits the ["Cache miss. Scan selecting objects"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138) path, iterating all HPA selectors in the BiMultimap. #### 3. title: Proposal: Request HPA to preinstall backup pods for minimizing service interruption upon failures
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce an optional parameter to the HPA configuration, for example `backupReplicas`, that would allow you to:

- Specify the exact number of backup pods the autoscaler should maintain alongside the nominal ones.
- Better monitor the average load against the _TARGETS_ thresholds via the _kubectl get hpa_ command.

The new structure of the HPA specification would look like:

```go
type HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec struct {
	ScaleTargetRef CrossVersionObjectReference
	MinReplicas *int32
	MaxReplicas int32
	Metrics []MetricSpec
	Behavior *HorizontalPodAutoscalerBehavior
	BackupReplicas *int32
}
```


### Why is this needed?

When a pod fails, Kubernetes might take time before restoring another pod on a new node. Deploying a new pod involves time-consuming operations like starting pod processes, downloading container images or sometimes waiting for an available node. Preprovisioning one or several shared backup pods in addition to the nominal ones can reduce the service interruption since those time-consuming operations are already achieved before the pod failure occurs.

Suppose that a Kubernetes service is configured to load balance flows onto a replicaset bound with an HPA defined with the `minReplicas` parameter equal to (_1_ + _Backup_) and with the `maxReplicas` parameter equal to (_Nominal_ + _Backup_). For the shared protection to be efficient, the HPA should add a (_x_ + _1_)<sup>th</sup> pod in the replicaset as soon as the pods are loaded at a ratio (_x_ - _Backup_) / _x_ that depends on _x_, the number of pods already deployed.

Based solely on fixed _TARGETS_ thresholds, the current `v2` HPA version does not satisfy this requirement. By introducing the optional `backupReplicas` parameter, the HPA can decide to add or remove a pod at the right pod load ratio and in this way become fully compatible with the shared protection requirement.

### What happened?

Bug description
kubectl cp fails on large files and leaving hanging tar zombie process inside the pod 
Scenario:
1. create a pod in k8s with attached pvc - or even with temporary file system.
2. create a large file of several GB inside the pod.
3. copy the pod from inside the pod to a target location where space is lacking.
4. the kubectl cp uses tar inside the pod and will fail due to not enough space.
5. the tar file will be hanging inside the pod .
6. file handle pointing to the file will stay 
7. If using pvc of cephfs - if somone deletes the file , the system does not see it but the cephfs has a stray file

the scenario will eventually cause a "leak" in ceph fs , and might consume all cluster data

title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection
body:
### What happened?

When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422.

Because the status update fails, the controller cannot:
- Flush `uncountedTerminatedPods`
- Remove `batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking` finalizers from terminated pods

This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale.

**Root cause:** Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active:

```go
// Location 1: global backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}

// Location 2: per-index backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}
```

The caller sets `job.Status.Active = active` (the returned 0), while `job.Status.Ready` stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: `5 > 0` → 422.

The `0` was likely a "don't care" value from before `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` validation existed. Every other return path in `manageJob` returns the real active count.

### What did you expect to happen?

The backoff early-return in `manageJob()` should return the real active pod count (unchanged, since no pods were created or deleted), not 0.

Proposed fix:
```diff
     if remainingTime > 0 {
         jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
-        return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
+        return active, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
     }
```

Returning `active` (initialized at top of `manageJob` as `int32(len(jobCtx.activePods))`) means "I didn't create or delete any pods" — the correct semantics for a backoff deferral.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
# 1. Create a Job
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: repro-ready-active
  namespace: default
spec:
  parallelism: 30
  completions: 30
  backoffLimit: 500
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "10m"
            memory: "16Mi"
EOF

# 2. Wait for all pods to be Running+Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active --timeout=120s

# 3. Force-delete 25 pods simultaneously
kubectl get pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active -o name | head -25 | \
  xargs -P25 kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0

# 4. Observe: job status is frozen, KCM logs show error
kubectl get job repro-ready-active -o jsonpath='active={.status.active} ready={.status.ready} failed={.status.failed}'
# Output: active=30 ready=30 failed=   (stale — doesn't reflect reality)

# KCM logs show:
# "Unhandled Error" err="syncing job: tracking status: adding uncounted pods to status:
#   Job.batch \"repro-ready-active\" is invalid: status.ready: Invalid value: 5:
#   cannot set more ready pods than active"

# 5. Bug self-resolves after ~10 min when backoff expires (if no new failures arrive)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The bug fires on any multi-pod Job that experiences a pod failure while other pods are still Ready. For single failures (10s backoff), it produces a few 422 errors that self-resolve. For mass failures (spot reclamation, node failure → backoff capped at 10 min), it causes visible stuck pods and stale status for the full backoff duration.

title: [Feature Request] Native Zone/Topology-Aware Scaling in HPA to complement Topology Aware Routing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Description
When combining **Topology Aware Routing** (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) with the **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**, there is a systemic architectural gap that risks localized pod starvation during scale-out events, and extreme endpoint imbalance during scale-in events. 

Currently, the HPA evaluates resource utilization (e.g., CPU, Memory) as a global, deployment-wide aggregate average. However, Topology Aware Routing deliberately isolates traffic to localized Availability Zones (AZs). 

This decoupled behavior creates a "Thundering Herd" trap during spikes, and a "Starvation" trap during downscaling, because the network routing layer is highly topology-aware while the autoscaling control loop is completely topology-blind.


### Why is this needed?


### Use Case
We run high-throughput microservices on AWS (EKS) distributed across 3 Availability Zones. To mitigate high cross-AZ data transfer costs ("Cross-AZ Tax") and lower network latency, we rely heavily on Topology Aware Routing. 

We face two distinct structural failures due to the lack of zone-aware autoscaling:

1. **The Scale-Out Trap (Localized Overload):** During localized network shifts or zone-specific traffic spikes, pods in a single AZ (e.g., `us-east-1a`) take 100% of that localized load. If `us-east-1a` pods hit 95% CPU utilization while pods in `us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c` remain idle at 10%, the cluster-wide average sits at ~38%. The HPA fails to trigger, and the pods in the stressed zone crash due to localized resource starvation.
2. **The Scale-In Trap (Zone Depletion):** When traffic drops globally and the HPA triggers a downscale event, the underlying ReplicaSet controller selects pods for termination without respecting zone distribution. It frequently terminates a disproportionate number of pods from a single zone. This leaves that specific zone entirely depleted of endpoints, breaking the path for subsequent localized traffic and forcing expensive, high-latency cross-AZ failovers.

### Proposed Solution / Architectural Approaches
We request native support for zone/topology-awareness within the core autoscaling and lifecycle framework:

1. **Topology-Aware Scale-Out Policy:** Introduce a configuration field in the HPA spec (e.g., `scalingPolicy.topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) that evaluates metrics per topology domain. If *any single zone* breaches the target utilization threshold, the HPA should proactively trigger a scale-up event.
2. **Topology-Aware Scale-In (Downscaling):** Ensure that when the HPA reduces the replica count, the scale-in mechanism balances pod terminations proportionally across all active topology domains. The controller must prevent downscaling from leaving a specific zone starved of healthy endpoints.
3. **Handling Soft Constraints (`ScheduleAnyway`):** If a deployment utilizes `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, a Zone-Aware HPA should exploit this flexibility. During a localized spike, it should scale up replicas specifically within the hurting topology domain, allowing a temporary skew to absorb the traffic. During the subsequent scale-in event, the controller must prioritize deleting pods from the skewed zone to automatically return the cluster to its baseline balanced topology spread.

### Related Existing Issue
* **kubernetes/kubernetes #124149** 


### Additional Context
Current ecosystem workarounds require engineers to deploy entirely independent, duplicated Deployments and HPAs per AZ (e.g., `frontend-az-a`, `frontend-az-b`). This completely breaks standard GitOps principles, bloat CI/CD pipelines, and forces rigid, static replica constraints. Native lifecycle zone-awareness is required to bridge the gap between how Kubernetes routes traffic and how it manages compute capacity.

title: PDB maxUnavailable cannot compute expectedPods when a pod's direct controller owner does not implement /scale but a scalable ancestor exists
body:
## What happened

The disruption controller computes `expectedPods` for a PDB using `maxUnavailable` by calling the `/scale` subresource on each matched pod's **direct** controller owner (`metav1.GetControllerOf(pod)` → scale lookup in `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go`, `getExpectedScale` / `getPodControllerFromScale`).

When the direct owner does not implement `/scale`, the lookup errors and the PDB falls back to `expectedPods: 0` → `disruptionsAllowed: 0`, emitting:

```
Warning  CalculateExpectedPodCountFailed
  Failed to calculate the number of expected pods:
  <resource> does not implement the scale subresource
```

This blocks **all** voluntary evictions for the protected pods, even when a *scalable* resource exists higher in the ownership chain.

## Why this matters beyond one project

This is a general limitation for any operator/CRD pattern with multi-level ownership, where the immediately-owning object is a per-instance (non-scalable) resource but a higher-level controller is scalable. A concrete, widely-deployed example is KubeVirt:

```
virt-launcher Pod  →  VirtualMachineInstance   (direct owner, NOT scalable)
                   →  VirtualMachine
                   →  VirtualMachinePool        (scalable — implements /scale)
```

`VirtualMachinePool` implements `/scale`, but the disruption controller never reaches it because it stops at the direct owner (`VirtualMachineInstance`). Result: `maxUnavailable` PDBs are unusable for these workloads and users must fall back to `minAvailable`. (See kubevirt/kubevirt#18063 for the downstream report.)

## Current behavior

`getExpectedScale` resolves only the direct `controllerRef` and attempts a single scale lookup against it. There is no traversal of the `ownerReferences` chain.

## Proposed enhancement

When the direct controller owner does not implement `/scale`, walk the `controllerRef` chain upward (`owner → owner-of-owner → …`) and use the **nearest ancestor that implements `/scale`** to compute `expectedPods`. Stop at the first scalable ancestor, or fall back to the current behavior if none exists.

Semantically this is correct: when many pods resolve to the same scalable ancestor (deduplicated by controller UID, as the controller already does), `expectedPods` becomes that ancestor's `scale.spec.replicas` — i.e. the real desired count of the workload the PDB is protecting.

### Open design questions (likely KEP material)

1. **Object lookups for intermediate owners.** Traversal requires GET-ing each intermediate owner object to read its `ownerReferences`. The disruption controller today only has typed finders for built-in workload types plus the polymorphic scale client. Walking arbitrary CRD chains needs a dynamic/metadata client and correspondingly broad RBAC. What is the right scoping (e.g. bounded depth, only follow `controller: true` refs)?
2. **Depth bound & cycle protection.** Cap traversal depth and guard against cyclic/malformed `ownerReferences`.
3. **Ambiguity.** If multiple matched pods resolve to *different* scalable ancestors, sum per-ancestor scales (the existing dedup-by-UID logic already handles this once ancestors are correctly identified).
4. **Backward compatibility.** Behavior only changes for pods whose direct owner is non-scalable today (currently a hard failure), so this is strictly an improvement — no regression for existing scalable-direct-owner cases.

## Alternatives considered

- **Implement `/scale` on the direct owner** (e.g. add it to the per-instance resource). Rejected as a general solution: it forces a `spec.replicas` field onto inherently-singleton resources and advertises horizontal scalability that does not exist, confusing HPA/`kubectl scale`/GitOps tooling.
- **Use `minAvailable`.** Works today and needs no change, but does not give users the `maxUnavailable` semantics they ask for. Acceptable workaround, not a fix.

body:
### What happened?

When a UDP service with active senders is scaled down to zero endpoints, the conntrack entries established while the endpoints existed are never removed. The conntrack reconciler introduced in v1.32 (#127318) skips services without serving endpoints:

```go
// pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go
// a Service without endpoints does not require to clean the conntrack entries associated.
if endpoints.Len() == 0 {
    continue
}
```

The `REJECT` rule installed for a service with no endpoints does not help for those pre-existing flows: packets are DNATed to the (deleted) endpoint IP by conntrack before the filter rule, which matches on the service ClusterIP, can be evaluated. For one-way UDP traffic (statsd/dogstatsd-style, conntrack entries permanently `[UNREPLIED]`), every packet refreshes the 30s `nf_conntrack_udp_timeout`, so the stale entries and the blackholed traffic persist indefinitely.

In our production case (statsd at ~64k pkt/s cluster-wide), all senders kept DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP for 13 hours. All that traffic converges on the node that owns the deleted pod IP's CIDR block and is dropped there in `NET_RX`, which held a single 8-core node at ~60-73% softirq for the whole duration. Recovery is instant once the service gets an endpoint again, because the reconciler then processes the service and deletes every entry whose reply-source is not the new endpoint.

Observed evidence on v1.33.5 (iptables mode, controlled reproduction, ~3.5 min after scaling to 0, kube-proxy already synced):

```
# REJECT rule is installed:
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.0.200.123/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/udp-sink:statsd has no endpoints" -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable

# yet the stale entry persists and keeps refreshing (pod 10.244.5.127 deleted minutes ago):
udp 17 29 src=10.244.9.181 dst=10.0.200.123 sport=12345 dport=9125 [UNREPLIED] src=10.244.5.127 dst=10.244.9.181 sport=9125 dport=12345

# reconciler ran but deleted nothing:
kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total{ip_family="IPv4"} 1151   # unchanged

# after scaling back to 1 replica: counter 1151 -> 1152, entry deleted, traffic restored instantly
```

This is a regression versus <=1.31: the event-based cleanup (`DeletedUDPEndpoints` in the pre-reconciler `CleanStaleEntries`) cleared entries for every deleted UDP endpoint regardless of how many endpoints remained, so the N->0 transition was covered.

### What did you expect to happen?

Scaling a UDP service to zero endpoints removes the conntrack entries DNAT-ing to the deleted endpoints, the same way scaling from N to M>0 does. New packets then hit the `REJECT` rule (which also prevents new conntrack entries from being confirmed), and senders receive ICMP port-unreachable instead of blackholing traffic to a deleted pod IP forever.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a UDP deployment + ClusterIP service (port 9125), 1 replica.
2. From a pod on a different node, send UDP to the ClusterIP from a single long-lived socket (fixed source port) at any steady rate, e.g. 5 pkt/s:
   `while true; do echo ping; sleep 0.2; done | nc -u -p 12345 <ClusterIP> 9125`
3. `kubectl scale deploy/<name> --replicas=0` and wait for the pod to be deleted.
4. On the sender's node, run `conntrack -L -p udp --orig-port-dst 9125`. The entry persists indefinitely (timeout refreshed by every packet), DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP, even though `iptables-save | grep "has no endpoints"` shows the REJECT rule. `kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total` does not increase.
5. `kubectl scale --replicas=1`: the entry is deleted on the next sync (counter increments), confirming the reconciler handles the service again as soon as it has an endpoint.

title: CronJob controller: processNextWorkItem does not call queue.Forget on the  (nil, nil) sync path, leaving stale rate-limiter backoff count
body:
[[sig-redacted]]

**Description**

In `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#processNextWorkItem` only resets the workqueue rate limiter (queue.Forget) inside the requeueAfter != nil branch. When sync() returns (nil, nil) — no error and no requeue — none of the switch branches run, so Forget is never called:

```
requeueAfter, err := jm.sync(ctx, key)
switch {
case err != nil:
    utilruntime.HandleError(...)
    jm.queue.AddRateLimited(key)
case requeueAfter != nil:
    jm.queue.Forget(key)
    jm.queue.AddAfter(key, *requeueAfter)
// err == nil && requeueAfter == nil: nothing runs, Forget is not called
}

return true

```

Some paths/conditions when nil, nil are returned are such as below:
- CronJob not found / already deleted (returned directly by sync)
- CronJob being deleted (DeletionTimestamp != nil)
- CronJob suspended (spec.suspend == true)
- invalid spec.timeZone
- unparseable or invalid spec.schedule


**Issue**
I took one example flow and say : 
Take a suspended CronJob: on any given sync it may or may not need a status write, and that write may or may not succeed.( in `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#syncCronJob` )
- Status write fails → sync returns (nil, err) → processNextWorkItem takes the err != nil branch → AddRateLimited increments the failure count.
- Status write succeeds → sync returns (nil, nil) → no branch runs → the count is left unchanged.

So the same path that can drive the counter up (when its status write errors) never brings it back down (when its status write succeeds).


**What happens if this isn't fixed**

I would be honest, i dont want to oversell this and the severity/impact might be on the lower side but there is definitely an impact.

Consider a CronJob that accumulated some failures during an API incident and is then suspended . Because the suspended sync returns (nil, nil), the stale failure count is retained. When the CronJob is later resumed and its first reconcile hits a transient error, AddRateLimited computes the backoff from the stale count rather than from a clean baseline.
Also - since queue keys by namespace/name, a later CronJob recreated with the same name inherits the previous object's stale backoff.

**Potential Fix**
Its just a simple one liner.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139918

**How was this uncovered**

In the sprit of full transparency :

I found this while building my own open source case study [tool](https://github.com/somak2kai/beats) on golang structural fingerprints and potential outliers and I used Kubernetes (among many others oss repos) as test subjects.  
processNextWorkItem in cronjob_controllerv2 was marked as a potential outlier compared to its cousins  such as the below ( and all of the below follow similar pattern of .forget on queue)
certificates/clustertrustbundlepublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
processNextWorkItem	rootcacertpublisher	certificates/rootcacertpublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/bootstrap/tokencleaner.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/certificates/certificate_controller.go#processNextWorkItem

The goal of the tool was not to find issues , but was to perform a case study. This particular issue stood out , hence raising it. No personal agenda behind this 🙏

title: Kubelet emits transient `object "<ns>"/"<name>" not registered` (FailedMount) on cold start
body:
## What happens

On kubelet start/restart (node reboot, kubelet upgrade, cold node join), pods that mount secret
or configMap volumes intermittently fail to mount with a `FailedMount` event:

```
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "sec" : object "bootrace-min"/"s37" not registered
```

It is transient and clears on the volume reconciler's next pass, but delays pod startup and
generates many `FailedMount` events at scale (node reboots, node-pool upgrades).

## Environment

- Kubernetes: reproduced on v1.31.14; symptom reported across 1.22–1.27 (see related issues).
- Node: 2 vCPU Linux, containerd, single-node kubeadm cluster.

## Reproduce

Small node (e.g. **2 vCPU**), kubelet `maxPods` raised to fit the pod count: create N pods each
mounting its **own distinct** secret + configMap, then restart kubelet a few times. A *shared*
object does not reproduce; the objects must be distinct.

```bash
./repro.sh                 # 150 distinct-object pods, 6 kubelet restarts (defaults)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.sh</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# USAGE: ./repro.sh [NUM_PODS] [RESTARTS] [SETTLE_SECS]   (defaults: 150 6 25)
# ENV:   NS, NODE, RESTART_CMD="sudo systemctl restart kubelet"
# Requires kubectl + ability to restart kubelet on the node. Raise kubelet maxPods to fit NUM_PODS.
set -uo pipefail
N="${1:-150}"; R="${2:-6}"; SETTLE="${3:-25}"
NS="${NS:-bootrace-min}"
RESTART_CMD="${RESTART_CMD:-sudo systemctl restart kubelet}"
NODE="${NODE:-$(kubectl get nodes --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '$2=="Ready"{print $1; exit}')}"
[ -z "$NODE" ] && { echo "ERROR: no Ready node; set NODE=<name>"; exit 1; }

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: Secret\nmetadata: {name: s%d, namespace: %s}\nstringData: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
    printf 'apiVersion: v1\nkind: ConfigMap\nmetadata: {name: c%d, namespace: %s}\ndata: {k: "v%d"}\n---\n' "$i" "$NS" "$i"
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null
{ for i in $(seq 1 "$N"); do cat <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: p$i, namespace: $NS, labels: {app: bootrace-min}}
spec:
  nodeName: $NODE
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
  tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: sec, mountPath: /etc/sec, readOnly: true}
    - {name: cm,  mountPath: /etc/cm,  readOnly: true}
  volumes:
  - {name: sec, secret: {secretName: s$i}}
  - {name: cm,  configMap: {name: c$i}}
---
EOF
  done; } | kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null

for t in $(seq 1 120); do
  run=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
  [ "$run" -ge "$N" ] && break; sleep 4
done
echo "Running: $run / $N"

total=0
for b in $(seq 1 "$R"); do
  kubectl -n "$NS" delete events --all >/dev/null 2>&1
  eval "$RESTART_CMD"
  sleep "$SETTLE"
  hits=$(kubectl -n "$NS" get events --field-selector reason=FailedMount \
           -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.message}{"\n"}{end}' 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'not registered')
  total=$((total + hits))
  printf 'restart %2d/%d | FailedMount "not registered": %d\n' "$b" "$R" "$hits"
done
echo "TOTAL 'not registered' FailedMount events: $total"
echo "Cleanup: kubectl delete ns $NS"
```
</details>

title: Possible user confusion from differing zpage information
body:
I've been look at the zpages support which went to beta in 1.36 ( [KEP-4828](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/[sig-redacted]/4828-component-flagz/README.md) ) and I wanted to provide some feedback on where I think the current design might cause some user confusion, based on differences in output between the `/configz` and `/flagz` output.

From reading the KEP and some testing I understand that the `/flagz` endpoint returns the values set by command line flags passed to the component *or* default values where no explicit configuration flag has been passed. In contrast to this `/configz` returns the running configuration of the component taking into account flags, default values, and configuration files.

As a result, where components have values set from configuration files as well as command line flags, the responses from `/flagz` and `/configz` will be different. Looking at a standard Kubeadm 1.36 cluster, in that setup it occurs in the kube-proxy and kubelet components, as the others either don't use configuration files (kube-scheduler and kube-controller) or don't have a `/configz` endpoint (kube-apiserver).

As an example in the kubelet there are several significant differences in what's returned by `/flagz` and `/configz`, some of them are :-

- `/flagz` reports that anonymous authentication is enabled for the kubelet, however this is disabled in the kubelets configuration file, so in reality it is not enabled.
- `/flagz` reports that the cgroupDriver is `cgroupfs` (this is the default, there's no explicit flag set by the component) but the configuration file sets `systemd` which is reported by `/configz`
- `/flagz` reports `rotate-certificates` is `false`, but this is enabled in the configuration file `rotateCertificates` setting.
  
This could be particularly tricky for the `kube-apiserver` as there is no `/configz` endpoints, so no obvious path for cluster admins to check the full running configuration. 

Currently in the [zpages documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/zpages/) there is no mention of `/configz` which may lead to cluster administrators being unaware of its presence or unaware of the difference in output between `/flagz` and `/configz`

As the goal of this feature is to support cluster administrators in diagnosing issues with running clusters, it would be great to explain the differences between these two endpoints, and ensure that they're available for all components.

title: kubectl: `cluster-info dump --output-directory` writes pod logs (with embedded secrets) as world-readable
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP` writes every dump file via `setupOutputWriter`, which does:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126 (func setupOutputWriter)
file, err := os.Create(fullFile)
```

`os.Create` opens files `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` with mode `0666` before umask. With the very common `0022` umask that is `0644` (world-readable); with `0002` (common on shared systems / some distros) it is `0664` (group- and other-readable). Parents are created `0755` (`os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)` at line 124), so the directory tree is traversable by "other".

Pod logs are dumped verbatim to `{DUMP}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt` (line 295 → `writer.Write(data)` at line 287, raw bytes straight from the `log` API). Pod logs routinely contain application secrets: bearer tokens, DB connection strings, cloud credentials, signed URLs, signed certificate/key material, etc.

### What did you expect to happen?

Dump files should be created owner-only (`0600`), and the dump directory tree owner-only (`0700`) when it contains pod logs or other potentially sensitive cluster state, so that an unprivileged local user cannot read the operator's cluster dump.

Preconditions on the victim host: another local user can traverse the path to DUMP (the typical case — DUMP in a home dir, `/tmp`, a shared scratch dir, or a CI artifact dir whose parents are `0755`). The attacker needs **no Kubernetes API credentials at all** — only filesystem read on files kubectl itself just created.

1. Authorized/privileged operator runs kubectl once:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP --all-namespaces
   ```
   kubectl creates DUMP and all nested dirs `0755`, and every `logs.txt` (and `nodes.txt`, `events.txt`, …) `0644`/`0664`, with full pod-log contents — across **all** namespaces requested.
2. A second unprivileged local user reads the logs directly:
   ```bash
   cat $DUMP/*/leaky/logs.txt        # 044-mode readable + traversable parents (0755) => readable by "other"
   ```
   No exploit primitive required — ordinary filesystem ACLs. `--all-namespaces` widens the blast radius to logs from every namespace, including ones the attacker has no RBAC right to read.
3. Extract whatever secret the logs leaked (token, password, cert+key), then use it against the cluster or upstream systems:
   ```bash
   kubectl --token=<LEAKED> ...        # if a bearer token was logged
   # or use a leaked DB connection string / cloud credential against the corresponding backend
   ```
   → access beyond the attacker's normal reach, often as a high-privilege workload identity.

Exposure is **durable**: the files persist at `0644`/`0664` on disk under DUMP until someone manually tightens permissions or deletes them, and re-running the dump re-creates them the same way. On a shared host captured by automation, the window can stay open indefinitely.

### What happened?

kubelet exposes its resolved `KubeletConfiguration` at the `/configz` endpoint. When kubelet is run with `--manifest-url` and `--manifest-url-header` carrying credentials (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values **are returned in cleartext** by `GET /configz`, with no masking.

The codebase already knows these values are secret: the internal type tags the field `datapolicy:"token"`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the **logging** path masks it before printing (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:288-291`):

```go
config := kubeletServer.KubeletConfiguration.DeepCopy()
for k := range config.StaticPodURLHeader {
    config.StaticPodURLHeader[k] = []string{"<masked>"}
}
logger.V(5).Info("KubeletConfiguration", "configuration", klog.Format(config))
```

But the **`/configz`** path does not. `setConfigz` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:558-569`) converts the *original, un-masked* internal config to the external `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration` and registers it:

```go
func setConfigz(cz *configz.Config, kc *kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration) error {
    scheme, _, err := kubeletscheme.NewSchemeAndCodecs()
    ...
    versioned := &kubeletconfigv1beta1.KubeletConfiguration{}
    if err := scheme.Convert(kc, versioned, nil); err != nil { return err }   // raw headers flow through
    versioned.GetObjectKind().SetGroupVersionKind(...)
    return cz.Set(versioned)
}
```

`configz` then serializes registered objects with plain `json.Marshal` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/configz/configz.go:129-145`), so the header values ship out verbatim. The v1beta1 field is a plain `map[string][]string` with no custom marshaler and no `datapolicy` tag, so nothing redacts it.

`/configz` is installed on kubelet's authenticated server (`pkg/kubelet/server/server.go:648`) and runs through the auth chain (`pkg/kubelet/server/auth.go:108-109`): with `KubeletFineGrainedAuthz` it maps to `nodes/configz`; otherwise it falls under `nodes/proxy`.

`/configz` should mask `StaticPodURLHeader` exactly as the logging path does (`server.go:288-291`) — on a deep copy before registration via `setConfigz`/`initConfigz` (`server.go:558-579, 775-776`), or omit the field from external JSON. The existing `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the logging mask express the intent; `/configz` silently bypasses both. Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

title: Job admission plugin checks gang-scheduling parallelism guard when only one of GenericWorkload/WorkloadWithJob is enabled
body:
<!-- This issue was generated with AI assistance -->

## What happened?

The `validateParallelismChange` admission check in `plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go` uses an AND condition to skip validation:

```go
if !p.genericWorkloadEnabled && !p.workloadWithJobEnabled {
    return nil
}
```

This means the gang-scheduling parallelism guard is active when **either** feature gate is enabled. Disabling only `WorkloadWithJob` (or only `GenericWorkload`) is not sufficient to bypass the check — both must be disabled.

If a user disables `WorkloadWithJob` expecting to opt out of gang-scheduling admission behavior, the check still fires because `GenericWorkload` is enabled (or vice versa).

## What did you expect to happen?

Disabling the relevant feature gate for the code path being exercised should be sufficient to skip the validation. For example, the `SchedulingGroup`-based path (line 133) only makes sense with `GenericWorkload`, and the owner-reference scan path (line 148) only makes sense with `WorkloadWithJob`. Each branch should be gated independently on its corresponding feature gate, rather than both branches being gated on the OR of the two gates.

## How can we reproduce it?

1. Disable `WorkloadWithJob` feature gate, leave `GenericWorkload` enabled.
2. Create a Job that has an owner-created PodGroup with gang scheduling.
3. Attempt to update the Job's parallelism.
4. Observe `is forbidden: cannot change parallelism for a Job referencing gang-scheduled PodGroup` even though `WorkloadWithJob` is disabled.

## Relevant code

`plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go`, `validateParallelismChange` function.

title: kubelet HTTP probe logs probe `httpHeaders` (Authorization / Cookie / API keys) at -v=4
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs an HTTP liveness/readiness/startup probe, it logs probe parameters at verbosity `-v=4` — and the logged fields include the raw `HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` values taken directly from the PodSpec:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go:160-173
case p.HTTPGet != nil:
    req, err := httpprobe.NewRequestForHTTPGetAction(p.HTTPGet, &container, status.PodIP, "probe")
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(4).Info("HTTP-Probe failed to create request", "error", err)
        return probe.Unknown, "", err
    }
    if loggerV4 := logger.V(4); logger.Enabled() {
        port := req.URL.Port()
        host := req.URL.Hostname()
        path := req.URL.Path
        scheme := req.URL.Scheme
        headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders              // <-- raw PodSpec headers
        loggerV4.Info("HTTP-Probe", "scheme", scheme, "host", host, "port", port,
            "path", path, "timeout", timeout, "headers", headers, "probeType", probeType)  // <-- sink
    }
    return pb.http.Probe(req, timeout)
```

`headers := p.HTTPGet.HTTPHeaders` is the user-supplied header list with **no redaction**, emitted into the `"headers"` structured field.

### What did you expect to happen?

The kubelet prober should not log raw probe `httpHeaders`. The `"headers"` field should be dropped or redacted (e.g. log only header names, or omit the value) in the `HTTP-Probe` line at `prober.go:173` — matching how other secret-bearing probe fields are handled. As written, attacker/operator-supplied credential headers are emitted verbatim into verbose logs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet/prober`, sets `-v=4`, builds an HTTP liveness probe with `Authorization: Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token`, calls the real `(*prober).runProbe`, and the fake HTTP prober returns `Success` — proving the leak happens **before** the request executes and does not require probe failure. Cleans up after itself; no cluster needed.

```bash

ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/prober/zz_poc_probe_header_leak_test.go"
SECRET="Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package prober

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"net/http"
	"testing"
	"time"

	v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"
	kubecontainer "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/container"
	"k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/probe"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSuccessHTTPProber struct{}

func (pocSuccessHTTPProber) Probe(_ *http.Request, _ time.Duration) (probe.Result, string, error) {
	return probe.Success, "ok", nil // probe SUCCEEDS — leak is pre-request, not failure-only
}

func TestPOCHTTPProbeHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	if flag.CommandLine.Lookup("v") == nil {
		klog.InitFlags(nil)
	}
	if err := flag.Set("v", "4"); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	pb := &prober{http: pocSuccessHTTPProber{}}
	_, _, err := pb.runProbe(
		context.Background(),
		liveness,
		&v1.Probe{ProbeHandler: v1.ProbeHandler{HTTPGet: &v1.HTTPGetAction{
			Path: "/healthz",
			Port: intstr.FromInt32(8080),
			HTTPHeaders: []v1.HTTPHeader{
				{Name: "Authorization", Value: "Bearer kubelet-probe-secret-token"},

## What happened?

`kubectl port-forward` unconditionally prints "Handling connection for <port>" to stderr on every connection.  There is no flag to suppress these messages.

A `--quiet` or `--verbosity` flag (or gating behind `-v` log levels) so users can suppress informational messages while preserving real errors on stderr.

Connect to localhost:5432 from another terminal.  Each connection prints:

Handling connection for 5432

There is no way to disable this without filtering all of stderr, which risks hiding real errors.

The message originates from a hardcoded `fmt.Fprintf(o.Out, "Handling connection for %d\n", port)` in `pkg/cmd/portforward/portforward.go` with no verbosity check.

title: kubectl: autocomplete --dry-run with '=' and value suggestions (none/server/client)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Improve shell completion for the `--dry-run` flag on mutating `kubectl` commands
(`apply`, `create`, `delete`, `patch`, `scale`, …) so that:

- `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>` completes to **`--dry-run=`** (with no trailing
  space and no file listing), and
- `kubectl apply --dry-run=<TAB>` suggests the valid values **`none` / `server` /
  `client`**.

**I'm working on this.** There is a cross-repo dependency: `--dry-run` carries an
optional value (it sets `NoOptDefVal` to support the deprecated bare `--dry-run`),
and cobra currently offers no way for a program to make a flag complete as
`--flag=`. I've opened an opt-in enhancement upstream in cobra to enable it:

- spf13/cobra#2433 — adds `Command.MarkFlagAppendEqual`

Once that lands and is vendored, the kubectl side is a small change in
`AddDryRunFlag` (registering value completion for `none/server/client` and
calling `MarkFlagAppendEqual("dry-run")`).

### Why is this needed?

For a flag with `NoOptDefVal` set, the only syntax that actually assigns a value
is `--dry-run=value`; `--dry-run value` (space-separated) treats `value` as a
positional argument and errors. Yet today `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>`
completes to `--dry-run ` (with a space) and then offers file completion, which:

- nudges users toward the non-working space-separated form, and
- gives no hint of the valid values (`none`, `server`, `client`).

Guiding users to `--dry-run=client` / `--dry-run=server` via completion makes the
flag more discoverable and steers them away from the deprecated bare `--dry-run`.

title: Using kubernetes/mount-utils ends up in re-formatting the filesystem
body:
### What happened?

Using [FormatAndMount](https://github.com/kubernetes/mount-utils/blob/d06d436a17294305776494aa876d6e8e38c9200c/mount.go#L189) library from kubernetes/mount-utils ends in re-formatting partially broken filesystem instead of failing erroring out. 

### What did you expect to happen?

If filesystem is partially broken (i.e primary superblock of filesystem got corrupted) instead of silently re-formatting the device library should error out.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It will be tricky to reproduce issue, but I will list steps:

Incident timeline: how a killed  fsck  leads to data loss

• **T0 — Initial provisioning**: The application (pod) is scheduled onto the node for the first time. During the  NodeStageVolume  request, the CSI driver formats the disk with a filesystem (ext4) and mounts it.
• **T1 — Data written, then there is reboot of node**: The application writes a significant amount of data. Before this data is fully flushed to disk, the node restarts unexpectedly, leaving the filesystem in a dirty (inconsistent) state.
• **T2 — Re-stage triggers fsck**: The node comes back online and the pod is rescheduled. The CSI node driver receives a fresh  NodeStageVolume  request for the same volume. Because it uses mount-utils'  FormatAndMount , it detects an existing filesystem and unconditionally runs  fsck  to repair it.
• **T3 — fsck killed mid-repair**: While  fsck  is still running, the node restarts again (or the  fsck  process is killed). Interrupting  fsck  mid-write can corrupt the filesystem's primary superblock.
• **T4 — Silent reformat wipes data**: The node comes back online and the driver receives another  NodeStageVolume  request. This time, the filesystem check reports no filesystem (because  blkid  can only read the now-corrupted primary superblock). Treating the disk as unformatted,  FormatAndMount  reformats it as ext4 — wiping all previously written data, even though the data was still recoverable via backup superblocks.

title: utilyaml: YAMLReader/YAMLOrJSONDecoder corrupts UTF-16 input, causing misleading "yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character"
body:
/kind bug
[[sig-redacted]]

### What happened?

`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml.YAMLOrJSONDecoder` (via the underlying `YAMLReader`/`LineReader`) corrupts UTF-16 encoded input: a valid, BOM'd UTF-16 LE YAML document comes out of `YAMLReader.Read()` one byte longer than it went in — an odd-length UTF-16 stream — and the downstream yaml parser then fails with `yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character`. The error blames the user's file for being truncated when the file is actually valid; the truncation is introduced by the reader itself.

The yaml parser is not at fault: go-yaml is a libyaml port and handles BOM'd UTF-16 natively — `yaml.v2`, `yaml.v3` and `sigs.k8s.io/yaml` all parse the same bytes fine when handed the unmangled stream.

The corruption is in `LineReader.Read()`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.36.2/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go#L447-L461

`bufio.Reader.ReadLine()` (L456) splits at the raw `0x0a` byte — a UTF-8 assumption — and strips it, then `buffer.WriteByte('\n')` (L459) re-appends a *single-byte* UTF-8 newline. Mid-stream this happens to round-trip: each two-byte `0a 00` newline loses its `0a` to `ReadLine`, gains a fresh `0a` from `WriteByte`, and the orphaned `00` leads the next line, so the bytes reassemble in order. But at EOF the orphaned final `00` comes back as one more "line" and gets its own appended `0a`, so the stream grows by one byte and every subsequent UTF-16 code unit boundary is intact except the total length is now odd. A 314-byte document exits the reader as 315 bytes ending `... 0a 00 0a`.

This is byte-for-byte the encoding Windows PowerShell 5.1 produces with a plain `>` redirect, so "I wrote a manifest on Windows and the controller says my YAML is broken" is the practical failure mode.

### What did you expect to happen?

One of:

- BOM-detected UTF-16 input parses successfully. There is 10-year-old precedent for exactly this: kubectl has transcoded UTF-16 at the file-reading layer since 2016 (#39008), and still does — https://github.com/kubernetes/cli-runtime/blob/master/pkg/resource/visitor.go#L558-L561 wraps every file in `unicode.BOMOverride(unicode.UTF8.NewDecoder())` before the decoder sees it. That protection lives only in cli-runtime's `FileVisitor`; every other consumer of `YAMLOrJSONDecoder`/`YAMLReader` (controllers, operators, anything decoding user-supplied streams) is exposed.
- Or an early, explicit error ("unsupported encoding: UTF-16; convert to UTF-8") instead of silent corruption plus a misleading parser error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Encode any valid manifest as UTF-16 LE with BOM (what PowerShell `echo ... > file.yaml` writes):

```console
$ { printf '\xff\xfe'; iconv -f UTF-8 -t UTF-16LE svc.yaml; } > svc-utf16.yaml
```

```go
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"os"

	utilyaml "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml"
)

func main() {
	data, _ := os.ReadFile("svc-utf16.yaml")

	var out map[string]interface{}
	err := utilyaml.NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder(bytes.NewReader(data), 4096).Decode(&out)
	fmt.Println("Decode err:", err)

	r := utilyaml.NewYAMLReader(bufio.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data)))
	chunk, _ := r.Read()
	fmt.Printf("reader in: %d bytes, out: %d bytes\n", len(data), len(chunk))
}
```

Output (apimachinery v0.36.2):

```
Decode err: error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character
reader in: 314 bytes, out: 315 bytes
```

The same file parses fine with `sigs.k8s.io/yaml.Unmarshal` directly, and with `kubectl apply -f` (thanks to the cli-runtime transcoder).

### Anything else we need to know?

Real-world sighting: this is the root cause of fluxcd/flux2#1126 (2021) — kustomize-controller validated user manifests through kustomize's legacy `kunstruct` factory, which delegates to `NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder`, and PowerShell-authored files failed with this exact error. title: kube-controller-manager panics (nil pointer dereference) when a StorageVersionMigration targets a resource not present in the RESTMapper
body:
### What happened?

Creating a `StorageVersionMigration` for a resource, then removing that resource from the cluster (e.g. deleting the CRD) while the migration is still pending, makes the `kube-controller-manager` panic and enter `CrashLoopBackOff`.

The storage-version-migrator controller's `sync` dereferences a nil `*schema.GroupVersionResource`:

```
E0714 13:08:33 "Observed a panic" panic="runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference"
	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator.(*SVMController).sync(...)
		pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator/storageversionmigrator.go:227
...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
```

In `sync`, `resourceFor` returns `(nil, false, nil)` when the resource is not in the RESTMapper (this is the normal "unknown resource" return, not an error), and the following line logs `gvr.String()` on that nil pointer:

```go
gvr, exists, err := resourceFor(svmc.restMapper, toBeProcessedSVM.Spec.Resource)
if err != nil { return err }
if !exists {
    logger.V(4).Info("resource does not exist in our rest mapper", "gvr", gvr.String()) // gvr is nil -> panic
    ...
}
```

`GroupVersionResource.String()` has a value receiver, so calling it on a nil pointer dereferences it. The arguments of `logger.V(4).Info(...)` are evaluated unconditionally, so this happens regardless of the log verbosity. The panic crashes the whole controller-manager (all controllers stop) until the offending `StorageVersionMigration` is removed.

Note: the sibling function in the same package (`ResourceVersionController.sync` in `resourceversion.go`) handles the exact same `!exists` case without touching `gvr`, which is what makes this look like an oversight.

### What did you expect to happen?

The controller should handle a missing resource gracefully (it already intends to: it requeues for up to one minute, then marks the migration failed) without panicking or crashing the controller-manager.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a cluster with the `StorageVersionMigrator` feature enabled and the `storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1` API served:

```bash
# 1. A CRD (migrating a CRD to a new storage version is a documented use case)
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: widgets.example.com}
spec:
  group: example.com
  names: {plural: widgets, singular: widget, kind: Widget, listKind: WidgetList}
  scope: Namespaced
  versions: [{name: v1, served: true, storage: true, schema: {openAPIV3Schema: {type: object}}}]
YAML

# 2. Request a storage version migration for that resource
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageVersionMigration
metadata: {name: migrate-widgets}
spec: {resource: {group: example.com, resource: widgets}}
YAML

# 3. Delete the CRD (it leaves the RESTMapper) while the migration is pending
kubectl delete crd widgets.example.com
```

Within ~30-60s the kube-controller-manager panics and goes into CrashLoopBackOff:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager   # restartCount increasing, CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl -n kube-system logs <kcm-pod> --previous | grep -A2 "nil pointer"
```

Removing the `StorageVersionMigration` (`kubectl delete storageversionmigration migrate-widgets`) lets the controller-manager recover.

A unit-level reproduction (fake client, no cluster) is also available if you want it.

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause is a single line (`gvr.String()` on a nil pointer). Trigger requires cluster-admin rights (StorageVersionMigration is cluster-scoped) plus the target resource disappearing from the RESTMapper, so this is not a privilege-escalation issue, but the crash takes down the entire controller-manager.

title: CEL map-list concatenation preserves duplicate new keys from the right operand
body:
### What happened?

Schema-aware CEL map-list concatenation keeps duplicate new keys from the right operand instead of merging them.

`addToMapList` builds an index for the left operand, but does not add a key to that index when it appends the first new element from the right operand. A later element with the same key is therefore appended again.

For a map list keyed by `key1,key2`, if `x.mapList` contains two existing entries, this expression currently produces four entries and preserves both values `9` and `10`:

```cel
x.mapList + [
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 9},
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 10},
]
```

This breaks the merge-by-key semantics implemented for `x-kubernetes-list-type: map`. CEL policies that construct or inspect associative lists can observe the wrong size/value. Mutation expressions can also emit duplicate map keys, causing the admission request to be rejected instead of applying the later value.

### What did you expect to happen?

The first new key from the right operand should be appended and indexed. A later element with that key should overwrite it in place, so the example has one `new,key` entry with value `10`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to `TestListAdd` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/common/values_test.go` using the existing `x.mapList` fixture:

```go
{
    name: "map list + literal list merges duplicate new keys",
    expression: "size(x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}]) == 3 && (x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}])[2].value == 10",
}
```

Then run:

```console
GOWORK=off go test ./pkg/cel/common -run TestListAdd -count=1
```

The case fails with `Expected true with typed values but got false` on current `master`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The behavior is in the map-list concatenation support merged by #140292. Updating `keyToIdx` immediately after appending a new key fixes the regression and makes the test pass.

title: kubectl explain: add an -o skeleton output format for a copy-pasteable YAML starting point
body:
cc @kubernetes/[sig-redacted]

## What would you like to be added?

A new `kubectl explain <type> -o skeleton` output format that renders a
resource's schema as a concise, editable YAML skeleton (field names with
placeholder values) instead of the verbose field-by-field prose that
`plaintext`/`plaintext-openapiv2` produce.

A companion `-o skeleton-comments` renders the same skeleton with short
inline `# ...` comments for fields that need explaining: `# required`,
`# enum: A|B|C`, `# map[string]string`, and a drill-down hint for fields
collapsed for depth (see below).

Example, `kubectl explain deployments.spec.template.spec.containers -o skeleton`:

```yaml
containers:
- name: "<required>"
  args:
  - ""
  command:
  - ""
  env: []
  envFrom: []
  image: ""
  imagePullPolicy: ""
  lifecycle: {}
  livenessProbe: {}
  ports: []
  readinessProbe: {}
  resources: {}
  securityContext: {}
  startupProbe: {}
  stdin: false
  stdinOnce: false
  terminationMessagePath: ""
  terminationMessagePolicy: ""
  tty: false
  volumeDevices: []
  volumeMounts: []
  workingDir: ""
```

Design notes:
- Placeholder values come from the schema's own `default`, else the first
  `enum` value, else `example`, else a type-appropriate zero value. A
  required field with none of those (typically a bare string) gets the
  literal `"<required>"` sentinel so it isn't mistaken for an intentionally
  empty optional field.
- The `status` subresource and server-managed `metadata` fields
  (`resourceVersion`, `uid`, `managedFields`, etc.) are omitted, since nobody
  hand-authors those.
- To keep output readable on resources with deep optional structure (Pod's
  `affinity`/`tolerations`/`securityContext`, CRD validation schemas), each
  optional field spends against a small budget before its own optional
  children collapse to a placeholder with a drill-down hint (e.g.
  `# optional, nested further -- see: kubectl explain pods.spec.affinity -o skeleton`).
  Required fields are free, so a load-bearing chain like
  `containers[].image` always expands regardless of depth.
- Implemented as one more template in the existing `pkg/explain/v2`
  template-based generator (same mechanism as `plaintext-openapiv2`), so it
  only touches the openapiv3 explain path.

## Why is this needed?

`kubectl explain` today is documentation-first: it's great for looking up
what a field means, but not for the common case of "I want to write a
Deployment/CRD manifest and need a skeleton to fill in." Today's next-best
alternatives (`kubectl create deployment ... --dry-run=client -o yaml`,
hand-copying from docs, or `explain --recursive`) either only cover a
handful of built-in kinds, produce output flooded with every field
regardless of relevance, or don't work at all for CRDs.

`-o skeleton` gives a fast, copy-pasteable starting point for any resource
the cluster serves an OpenAPI v3 schema for, including CRDs, while staying
short enough to read. The optional-depth budget means you see the fields
that actually need decisions (`containers[].image`) without also seeing
every leaf of `affinity`/`tolerations` you probably don't need today, and
you can always drill into a collapsed field with a normal
`explain <type>.<field> -o skeleton` call.

This is proposed as a proof of concept with a working implementation and
test suite already in hand (unit tests covering required/optional
ordering, enums, maps, `$ref` cycles, field-path drill-down, and the
depth-budget behavior). Happy to open the PR once there's [sig-redacted] agreement
on the approach/flag naming.

title: CRD with identical per-version selectableFields but differing per-version schemas is rejected due to internal hoisting
body:
### What happened?

Creating a multi-version `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` CRD that declares the **same** `selectableFields` on two served versions whose **schemas differ** is rejected by the apiserver:

```
The CustomResourceDefinition "widgets.example.com" is invalid:
spec.selectableFields: Invalid value: "": may only be set when validations.schema is included
```

The error is doubly confusing: the manifest sets only `spec.versions[*].selectableFields` (valid per the v1 API), yet the error references top-level `spec.selectableFields` — a field that does not exist in the v1 API the user submitted.

**Root cause (from reading the source):** `Convert_v1_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec_To_apiextensions_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec` (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/conversion.go`) hoists each of the four per-version fields (`subresources`, `schema`, `additionalPrinterColumns`, `selectableFields`) to the internal top-level spec **independently**, whenever that field is identical across all versions. So with identical `selectableFields` but differing schemas:

- `selectableFields` **is** hoisted to internal `spec.SelectableFields` (and cleared per-version),
- `schema` is **not** hoisted (internal `spec.Validation` stays nil),

and internal validation then rejects the combination the conversion itself created (top-level `selectableFields` requires a top-level `validations.schema`). The user's input was never invalid; the independent hoisting manufactured the invalid internal state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Per-version `selectableFields` to be accepted on any served version, independent of whether the other versions' schemas are identical. KEP-4358 field selectors are declared per-version in v1; whether two versions happen to share a schema should not change the validity of identical selector declarations.

**Real-world impact:** any multi-version CRD mid-graduation — the standard pattern of serving two versions where the newer one drops deprecated fields — cannot offer the same field selector on both served versions. We hit this graduating a CRD whose new version removes two deprecated fields; controllers watching via field selector on the old version could not keep the selector when the new version was added. Workarounds: declare `selectableFields` on only one version (losing field selectors on the others), or keep the version schemas byte-identical (defeating the point of graduation).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this CRD:

```yaml

kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: widgets.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: widgets
    singular: widget
    kind: Widget
    listKind: WidgetList
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    selectableFields:
    - jsonPath: .spec.name
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              name: {type: string}
              extra: {type: string}   # <- v1-only field: schemas differ
  - name: v2
    served: true
    storage: false
    selectableFields:
    - jsonPath: .spec.name
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              name: {type: string}
```

→ rejected with the error above.

| per-version schemas | selectableFields | result |
|---|---|---|
| differ | on one version only | accepted |
| differ | identical on both | **rejected** |
| identical | identical on both | accepted (both hoist together) |

The identical-schemas row confirms the failure is the hoisting *interaction*, not the field declarations themselves.

title: DRA: Allocator reads device counter consumption from possibly modified slice
body:
### What happened?

/kind bug
[[sig-redacted]]
[[sig-redacted]]
/wg device-management

The structured allocator derives per-pool state about already-allocated devices from the current ResourceSlice contents. Slices are mutable, so a driver can republish a pool without a previously-allocated device, or with different `ConsumesCounters` for it - and when that happens, the allocated device's contribution silently disappears from the allocator's accounting. This affects two features with different severity:

**1. PartitionableDevices: counter availability can be over-committed.**

`checkAvailableCounters` (`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, mirrored in the incubating and stable allocators) computes per-pool availability by starting from the counter set totals and subtracting the consumption of allocated devices **found in the current slices**. An allocated device that is no longer published (or whose `ConsumesCounters` changed) no longer subtracts anything, so the pool appears to have more counters free than it physically does, and new allocations can over-commit the shared counters of a device that is still in use. 

**2. DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139795): the enforcement baseline loses allocated peers.**

`compatibilityGroupsBaselineForPool` deliberately copies the counters pattern (its comment: "exactly like checkAvailableCounters does for counters"): group *values* come from the allocation-time snapshot in the claim status, but counter-set *membership* still comes from the current slice. If the allocated device is not in the republished slice, its intersection contribution drops out of the feature-on baseline and a later incompatible device can be admitted onto the counter set. Notably, the feature-off version-skew skip (`groupedCounterSetsFromState`) is built purely from snapshots and keeps protecting the same counter set - the enforcement path is less conservative than the skip path.

### What did you expect to happen?

Accounting and enforcement for already-allocated devices should depend only on allocation-time state, never on the current slice contents, which the compatibility-groups KEP already designates as unsafe for enforcement (that is the snapshot's entire purpose).
